canonical_topic: Fair Value and core accounting terms
definition: Fair value is the amount of cash that would be required to liquidate (settle) an asset or liability under current market conditions; mark-to-market is one specific application of this broader fair-value approach.
core_idea: Fair value accounting rests on the premise that an item can actually be transferred for cash: something you'd be paid to hand over is an asset, something you'd have to pay someone to take off your hands is a liability, and the ease/cost of making that conversion to cash is its liquidity.
key_points: Mark (verb): to record something for accounting purposes.
Market: a mechanism (exchange or brokerage) that lets participants convert assets or liabilities into cash.
Asset: a financial instrument a third party would pay money to take ownership of.
Liability: a financial instrument that requires paying someone to take ownership of it.
Liquidation: the act of converting an asset or liability into cash.
Liquidity: how easily and cheaply something converts to cash — liquid instruments convert quickly and cheaply, illiquid ones do not.
Fair value is found by multiplying the quantity of an asset by its price per unit.
relationships: Fair value accounting is the umbrella category that mark-to-market accounting falls under.

formulas.name: Fair Value
formulas.formula: Fair Value = Quantity × Price per unit

variables.Price per unit: current market price for one unit
